transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-08 14:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Silverwood, Head of Infrastructure), Elena Ruiz (Silverwood, Security Engineer), Tom Baines (Silverwood, Platform Eng)

Summary: quick discovery on private VPC deployment, network topology options, region constraints and security integrations.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. i'm maya from redwood, ae on the account.
[00:12] Raj Patel: hey maya, morning. thanks, yeah we put a few folks on who care about network and security.
[00:18] Elena Ruiz: hi all, elena here, security. quick thing up front — we can't have public egress for inference requests, need private-only endpoints.
[00:26] Liam O'Connor: understood, elena. i'm liam, solution engineer, i'll walk through how our private deployment can sit inside your vpc and options for peering / private endpoints.
[00:38] Tom Baines: cool. one quick context note — we're on aws primarily, using multiple accounts per env, transit gw, and we have residency constraints in eu-west-1 for some customers.
[00:50] Maya Chen: perfect, that's helpful. to kick off — can you summarize the top three requirements you have for this integration?
[00:58] Raj Patel: sure. 1) private-only ingress/egress — no public internet paths. 2) control of KMS keys for model data in flight and at rest, ideally customer-managed keys. 3) low latency from eu-west-1 and us-east-1 customers, potential multi-region failover.
[01:18] Elena Ruiz: and add audit logs forwarded to our splunk, and SSO via SAML to our okta tenant. also we need SOC2 documentation and penetration test reports.
[01:29] Liam O'Connor: that'll all be covered; we have KMS integrations and support for customer-managed keys (we call out HSM/KMS options), and logging can be forwarded via syslog or s3 sinks depending on your retention.
[01:41] Maya Chen: on the private endpoints piece, do you have a preference — cross-account vpc peering, aws privatelink (endpoint services), or using a transit gateway?
[01:52] Tom Baines: transit gw is what we use today, but peering is simpler for small meshes. our infra team is wary of additional endpoint services for cost reasons.
[02:03] Liam O'Connor: tradeoffs — peering is straightforward but doesn't scale well if you have many accounts; transit gw is our recommended pattern for enterprise scale because it's easier to centralize. privatelink gives you by-default private connectivity without needing route table changes, but you do incur endpoint pricing and we need to publish an endpoint service from our side — that works cross-account too.
[02:25] Raj Patel: ok, so if we go transit gw, how does routing work? do we need to publish routes from our side to your subnets? what's the security boundary?
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: good q. in our private deployment model, we run Redwood control plane in your VPCs or in a customer-managed VPC? (crosstalk)
[02:44] Maya Chen: i'll just clarify — for Private we can offer two patterns: 1) customer-managed VPCs where components run in your accounts (we provide AMIs / helm charts and assist deployment), or 2) Redwood-managed private VPCs that peer with your accounts — both support transit gw or privatelink.
[03:02] Tom Baines: customer-managed preferred if possible — gives us full control over security posture.
[03:08] Elena Ruiz: agree, also for compliance we want keys in our KMS and logs flowing to our SIEM.
[03:14] Liam O'Connor: in customer-managed, you control subnets, route tables, and security groups. we'd provide a network diagram and list of required ports (eg 443 for grpc/http, plus ranges for health checks and internal control plane). we also recommend nat for any egress we cannot avoid, but you said no public egress?
[03:31] Raj Patel: correct — no public egress for inference traffic. management plane can have tightly controlled egress to specific redwood endpoints if necessary, but ideally everything is within private links.
[03:42] Liam O'Connor: right — we can set up privatelink endpoints so control plane APIs are available via interface endpoints in your VPC. that avoids internet egress. we also support VPC peering to our managed VPC if you prefer.
[03:56] Maya Chen: elena, you mentioned KMS. do you require AWS KMS CMKs, or would you accept envelope encryption with keys in our HSM?
[04:05] Elena Ruiz: we prefer AWS KMS CMKs with key policies restricting access to specific roles. HSM is okay for certain regs but harder.
[04:13] Liam O'Connor: we support customer-managed KMS. we can configure our services to use your CMK for model artifacts at rest and TLS keys can be rotated via a cert manager integrated with your key store.
[04:25] Raj Patel: what about network CIDRs? we've got fixed /16s per env and want to avoid overlap.
[04:31] Liam O'Connor: important point. we'll need your CIDR ranges to ensure no overlap; if we're running in your account you choose the subnets. if we're in a Redwood-managed VPC we'll provide recommended ranges and ask you to approve.
[04:44] Tom Baines: any special ports for kv cache or batching? we run a strict egress firewall.
[04:50] Liam O'Connor: main ports are 443 and ephemeral ranges for grpc, and internally we use some tcp ranges for cache sync — we'll put exact port list in the checklist.
[05:00] Maya Chen: quick demo of typical network topologies? (brief screen share note)
[05:08] Liam O'Connor: sure, so simple pattern: privatelink -> interface endpoint in your VPC -> target NLB or ENI in our service. second pattern is transit gw where you attach our managed account as a spoke and advertise routes. third is direct peering for small setups.
[05:30] Raj Patel: latency — we need p95 token latency under 300ms for eu-west-1. what options do we have to meet that?
[05:40] Liam O'Connor: we can co-locate inference pools in eu-west-1 and pin routing to that region. for multi-region failover we mirror model artifacts to a secondary region; that increases storage needs but keeps latency low.
[05:54] Elena Ruiz: mirror model artifacts — is that encrypted with our CMK as well?
[05:58] Liam O'Connor: yes, replication is encrypted and can be tied to a customer-managed key in each region.
[06:05] Tom Baines: what's the sequence for a peering test? we'd like to get an end-to-end test before committing to prod.
[06:12] Liam O'Connor: typical: 1) exchange CIDRs and account IDs, 2) create peering or TGW attachments, 3) install a small pilot with a single model, 4) run JMeter-style load and measure p95/p99, 5) iterate on security groups and NACLs.
[06:30] Raj Patel: fine — could you give an example of the CIDR avoidance matrix you need?
[06:35] Liam O'Connor: we'll send a spreadsheet — columns: account id, region, vpc cidr, public/private subnets, nat gateway present? and whether TGW is used.
[06:46] Elena Ruiz: on compliance docs — SOC2 reports, pen test summaries, and our legal needs an indemnification clause. do you have an enterprise kit?
[06:55] Maya Chen: yes, we'll send the security pack, SOC2 type ii, and our standard data processing addendum. legal can follow up on indemnification; we typically have enterprise terms for private deployments.
[07:07] Raj Patel: what about egress for model updates — we push models from our CI to the hosting region. how do you accept model pushes securely?
[07:16] Liam O'Connor: we support S3-based ingestion over privatelink endpoints or SFTP over private channels; authentication via IAM roles or short-lived certs. we can also pull from your private S3 via VPC endpoints.
[07:31] Tom Baines: any known gotchas with Transit Gateway and route propagation? we've had issues where TGW associated route tables didn't advertise specific prefixes.
[07:40] Liam O'Connor: yes, route propagation and blackhole routes are common. during the pilot we'll validate route tables and ensure the TGW attachments and propagation are set for the right associations. we'll include test scripts to validate.
[07:53] Elena Ruiz: wondering about key rotation — if we rotate CMKs, will that break access to past model artifacts?
[07:59] Liam O'Connor: no, rotations are handled via key aliasing; for cross-region replication we recommend a rotation plan that ensures access is retained during the window. we'll document recommended rotation cadence.
[08:12] Maya Chen: switching to plan and pricing briefly — private deployments have a base platform fee + infra costs if Redwood manages resources; customer-managed avoids infra fees but has professional services.
[08:24] Raj Patel: cost note captured. our procurement will want line items for transit gw endpoints and privatelink.
[08:31] Maya Chen: we'll include a sample TCO with endpoint costs.
[08:34] (short pause / crosstalk)
[08:40] Tom Baines: one more thing — can you support azure and gcp for DR? we have services in both clouds.
[08:47] Liam O'Connor: yes, we support multi-cloud private deployments, but cross-cloud peering typically uses vpn or cloud interconnect partners. for DR we can mirror artifacts to a gcp region and use private connectivity via partner links.
[08:59] Elena Ruiz: are there any limitations on size of model artifacts with private endpoints? we've got a 20GB custom model.
[09:06] Liam O'Connor: large artifacts are fine — we chunk and resume. if you're pushing from on-prem we recommend direct connect / expressroute for efficiency.
[09:15] Raj Patel: ok sounds good. next steps recap?
[09:20] Maya Chen: i'll recap: 1) i'll send architecture checklist, security pack, pricing TCO; 2) liam will send peering test plan and port lists; 3) elena to share CIDR blocks and compliance checklist; 4) schedule technical deep dive next week for hands-on peering test.
[09:37] Elena Ruiz: yep that works.
[09:39] Tom Baines: i'll block time for the 15th.
[09:42] Maya Chen: awesome — thanks everyone. we'll follow up by email with artifacts.
[09:47] Raj Patel: thanks all.

(End of transcript)

Notes: transcription contains a few imperfect transcriptions (privatelink sometimes transcribed as 'private link', transit gw as 'transit g.w.' etc.)
